summary: Specifies version 1.3 of Datagram Transport Layer Security, which lets applications communicate over datagram transports while preventing eavesdropping, tampering, and message forgery. It is based on TLS 1.3 and gives equivalent security guarantees, except for protection against reordering or replay of messages. It obsoletes RFC 6347.

eli5.summary: It is a way to send letters that nobody can read or change on the way, even when some letters arrive late or get lost.

questions: how does dtls handle packet loss
what is the dtls cookie exchange
subtitle: TLS 1.3 adapted for datagrams: the same security, but built to survive lost, reordered and duplicated packets.

tldr.problem: TLS needs a reliable, in-order transport, but applications that run over UDP still need protection against eavesdropping, tampering and forgery.
tldr.mechanism: DTLS 1.3 takes the TLS 1.3 handshake and adds record sequence numbers and epochs, handshake fragmentation, retransmission timers with ACK messages, and a cookie exchange to counter denial-of-service attacks.
tldr.outcome: It gives TLS 1.3-equivalent security except for order protection and guaranteed replay protection, and it obsoletes DTLS 1.2 (RFC 6347). It has since been updated by RFC 9853.

today: RFC 9147 is a Proposed Standard. It obsoletes RFC 6347 (DTLS 1.2) and has been updated by RFC 9853.

sections.title: TLS for Datagrams
sections.content:
TLS protects a channel between two peers, but it must run over a reliable transport, typically TCP. DTLS was developed for applications that use UDP. It is deliberately kept as similar to TLS as possible, to minimize new security invention and maximize code reuse.

DTLS 1.0 was defined as a delta from TLS 1.1 and DTLS 1.2 as a delta from TLS 1.2. There is no DTLS 1.1, because that version number was skipped to harmonize with TLS. RFC 9147 describes DTLS 1.3 as a delta from TLS 1.3 and obsoletes DTLS 1.2. Implementations that speak both DTLS 1.2 and 1.3 can interoperate with those that speak only DTLS 1.2. The RFC states that DTLS 1.0 is not recommended and is forbidden by RFC 8996.

DTLS keeps datagram behaviour: it does not compensate for lost or reordered application data. That suits delay-sensitive uses such as media streaming, Internet telephony and online gaming.
sections.eli5: DTLS is the lock-and-key system from TLS, rebuilt for mail that is dropped in a bin without any promise it arrives.

sections.title: Why TLS Cannot Be Used Directly
sections.content:
The RFC gives four reasons TLS does not work as is over datagrams, and what DTLS does about each.

  • TLS relies on an implicit record sequence number, which breaks as soon as a record is lost. DTLS adds sequence numbers to records.
  • The TLS handshake is lock-step. DTLS adds message sequence numbers so lost or reordered messages can be handled.
  • Handshake messages can be bigger than one datagram. DTLS adds a fragment offset and fragment length so messages can be split and reassembled.
  • Datagram protocols invite denial-of-service abuse. DTLS adds a return-routability check using the TLS 1.3 HelloRetryRequest.

Packet loss is handled with a simple retransmission timer. Reordering is handled by queueing out-of-order handshake messages. Replay detection is optional and uses a bitmap window of received records, as in IPsec AH and ESP, because duplicate packets are not always malicious.
sections.eli5: Mail that can get lost or shuffled needs page numbers, a way to cut long letters into pieces, and a check that the sender really lives at the return address.

sections.title: Records, Headers and Epochs
sections.content:
DTLS 1.3 uses two record forms: DTLSPlaintext for unprotected records and DTLSCiphertext for protected ones. The protected form has a short, variable-length unified header. Its first byte begins with the bits 001, followed by flags: C (Connection ID present), S (sequence number is 16 bits rather than 8) and L (a 16-bit length field is present), then the low two bits of the epoch. If the length is omitted, the record must be the last in its datagram.

Receivers sort records by their first byte. Alert (21), handshake (22) and ack (26) are plaintext. Other values are treated as ciphertext if the leading bits are 001, and otherwise rejected. IANA therefore reserved the content type range 32 to 63.

An epoch identifies one set of keys. Sequence numbers restart at 0 in each epoch. In DTLS 1.3 the record sequence numbers are also encrypted, using a mask derived from the first 16 bytes of the ciphertext, which prevents trivial tracking of sequence patterns. Each record must fit in a single datagram, and the record layer should help the application respect the path MTU.
sections.eli5: Each sealed envelope has a tiny label saying which key was used and which number it is. The number is itself scrambled so snoops cannot follow along.

sections.title: The Handshake and Cookie Exchange
sections.content:
DTLS 1.3 reuses the TLS 1.3 handshake messages and flows. Three things change: handshake headers gain message_seq, fragment_offset and fragment_length; retransmission timers are added; and a new ACK content type is added for reliable delivery. The TLS 1.3 compatibility mode is not used: servers must not echo legacy_session_id and endpoints must not send ChangeCipherSpec.

To resist attackers who exhaust server resources or use it as an amplifier, the server can answer a ClientHello with a HelloRetryRequest that carries a stateless cookie. The client must repeat its ClientHello with the cookie. This forces the client to be able to receive packets at its claimed address. It does not defend against attacks from valid addresses. Servers SHOULD perform the exchange by default, and clients must be prepared for it on every handshake. DTLS 1.3 no longer uses the DTLS 1.2 HelloVerifyRequest.

A server that skips the cookie exchange, for example with 0-RTT data, should limit what it sends toward an unverified address to three times the amount the client sent. The legacy_version field is always set to {254, 253} and real versions are negotiated with supported_versions, where 0xfefc means DTLS 1.3.
sections.eli5: Before telling you its secrets, the server sends a ticket to the address you gave. If you can bring the ticket back, it knows you really live there.

sections.title: Flights, Retransmission and ACKs
sections.content:
Handshake messages are grouped into flights: a flight starts with one peer's transmission and ends with the expected response. Each flight is driven by a four-state machine: PREPARING, SENDING, WAITING and FINISHED. Clients start in PREPARING and servers in WAITING.

Unless there is better information, implementations SHOULD start with a retransmit timer of 1000 ms and double it at each retransmission, up to no less than 60 seconds. For DTLS-SRTP the RFC recommends a default of 400 ms. DTLS stacks should not send more than 10 records in a single transmission, since there is no built-in congestion control.

The ACK message (content type 26) lists the record numbers of handshake records an endpoint has received and processed. ACKs allow selective, early retransmission after a sign of disruption. They are mandatory to confirm the last flight of a handshake and post-handshake messages such as NewSessionTicket. Handshake fragments may overlap, but senders must not change message bytes on retransmission.
sections.eli5: If you do not hear back in a second, you send the page again and wait twice as long next time. The other side can also say 'got pages 1 and 3', so you resend only page 2.

sections.title: Key Updates and Connection IDs
sections.content:
Like TLS 1.3, a DTLS 1.3 endpoint sends a KeyUpdate message to change its sending keys. The message must be acknowledged, and the sender must not use the new keys or send another KeyUpdate until the ACK arrives. Receivers keep the old keys until a message arrives that uses the new ones. Each update moves to a new epoch, and senders must not let the epoch exceed 2^48-1.

If the connection_id extension was negotiated, either side can send a NewConnectionId message with a list of CIDs and a usage of cid_immediate or cid_spare, and can ask for more with RequestConnectionId. Endpoints should use a new CID when sending on a new path, which helps privacy in multihomed cases. Only one message of each of these types may be outstanding, and an excessive number of requests can be met with the too_many_cids_requested alert (number 52).

Key derivation uses the label prefix dtls13 instead of tls13 , which keeps DTLS 1.3 and TLS 1.3 keys separate.
sections.eli5: Now and then the two sides agree to change the lock on their secret box, and they confirm it worked before throwing the old key away. They can also swap name tags so nobody can follow them.

sections.title: Security Considerations and Limits
sections.content:
With the exception of order protection and non-replayability, DTLS 1.3 has the same security guarantees as TLS 1.3. TLS always provides order protection and non-replayability. DTLS does not provide order protection and may not provide replay protection. DTLS replay protection is a per-record option and is separate from TLS's requirement to protect 0-RTT data.

Unlike TLS, DTLS should silently discard invalid records instead of ending the connection. If alerts are used they must be fatal, but over UDP this is not recommended because forgery is so easy. Because DTLS ignores records that fail authentication, forgers get multiple attempts, so implementations MUST count failures per key. The limit for AEAD_AES_128_GCM, AEAD_AES_256_GCM and AEAD_CHACHA20_POLY1305 is 2^36 records that fail authentication. TLS_AES_128_CCM_8_SHA256 must not be used without additional safeguards against forgery.

Cookies must depend on the client's address and be impossible for others to forge, and the cookie secret should be rotated. The cookie exchange gives no protection when connection ID endpoints change addresses, so implementations must not switch to a new address without a reachability test, and the RFC defines no such test.
sections.eli5: Because the letters can be shuffled or repeated, DTLS cannot promise the order, but it still keeps strangers from reading or changing them, and it counts bad forgeries so a pest cannot keep trying forever.
